references.text: The same instruction to wash the entrails and legs with water is repeated for burnt offerings of small livestock.
The description of the burnt offering as 'a pleasing aroma to the Lord' is repeated for bird offerings.
The burnt offering is described as 'a pleasing aroma, a fire offering to the Lord' at the consecration of priests.
The fire offering as 'a pleasing aroma to the Lord' is mentioned in connection with priestly ordination.
Noah's sacrifice is described as 'the pleasant fragrance' that the Lord smelled, the first reference to fragrant sacrifices.
Moses washed the entrails and legs with water at the consecration of Aaron and his sons.
The fire offering as 'a pleasing aroma to the Lord' is mentioned in connection with various types of offerings.
The daily burnt offering is described as 'a fire offering for a pleasing aroma to the Lord'.
Ezekiel describes the restored temple where burnt offerings are to be brought forward on the altar.
Paul uses the imagery of sacrifice and describes Christ's offering as 'a fragrant gift and an offering to God' (εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας).
Both verses emphasize that the ritual burning of the sacrifice creates 'a fragrance that pleases the Lord', regardless of whether it is a burnt or sin offering.
It reuses the same theological logic that ritual burning creates 'a fragrance that pleases the Lord', which strengthens the understanding of the acceptability of the sacrifice.
